questions.question: What is a Private IP address in AWS?
questions.answer: A private IP address is automatically assigned to every EC2 instance when launched inside a VPC. It is used only for internal communication within the same network. It is not routable on the public internet — no one outside the VPC can reach an instance using its private IP. Private IPs come from the RFC 1918 ranges (10.x.x.x, 172.16-31.x.x, 192.168.x.x).

questions.question: What is a Public IP address in AWS, and what is its limitation?
questions.answer: A public IP address is a globally routable IP assigned to an EC2 instance so it can communicate with the internet through the Internet Gateway. In AWS, the public IP is assigned by AWS (which acts as your ISP). The key limitation is that standard public IPs are ephemeral — they change every time you stop and start the instance. This means DNS records and firewall whitelists can break after a restart.

questions.question: What is an Elastic IP, and why is it used?
questions.answer: An Elastic IP (EIP) is a static public IPv4 address allocated to your AWS account. Unlike a standard public IP, it does not change when the instance is stopped and started. It is used when you need a predictable, fixed public IP — for example, for DNS records, customer firewall whitelisting, or production server IPs. It can also be moved between instances for fast failover. AWS charges for EIPs that are allocated but not associated with a running instance.

questions.question: What are the three RFC 1918 private IP ranges?
questions.answer: RFC 1918 defines three private IP ranges: 10.0.0.0/8 (the 24-bit block, ~16.7 million IPs), 172.16.0.0/12 (the 20-bit block, ~1 million IPs), and 192.168.0.0/16 (the 16-bit block, ~65,536 IPs). AWS VPCs most commonly use the 10.0.0.0/8 range because it provides the largest address space.

questions.question: How many IPs does AWS reserve in each subnet, and why?
questions.answer: AWS reserves 5 IP addresses in each subnet: the first address (network address), the second (VPC router), the third (DNS), the fourth (reserved for future use), and the last (broadcast). So a /24 subnet has 256 addresses but only 251 are usable for EC2 instances.

questions.question: What is a Bastion Host, and how does it work?
questions.answer: A Bastion Host (also called a Jump Server) is an EC2 instance placed in a public subnet that serves as a secure gateway to access EC2 instances in private subnets. The admin SSHs from their laptop into the Bastion Host (which has a public or Elastic IP), and then from the Bastion, SSHs into the private EC2 using its private IP. The private EC2 never needs a public IP — only the Bastion is exposed to the internet.

questions.question: What is AWS Systems Manager Session Manager, and why is it preferred over Bastion Host?
questions.answer: Session Manager is a feature of AWS Systems Manager that allows you to connect to EC2 instances without SSH keys, without open port 22, and without a Bastion Host. The SSM Agent on the EC2 makes an outbound HTTPS connection to the SSM service. It is preferred because it is more secure (no open ports), fully managed, provides built-in audit logging to CloudTrail and S3, and does not require managing SSH keys or a separate EC2 instance.

questions.question: What is a NAT Gateway?
questions.answer: NAT Gateway is a fully managed AWS service that allows EC2 instances in private subnets to initiate outbound connections to the internet (e.g., for software updates) without being directly reachable from the internet. It translates the private IP of the EC2 to its own Elastic IP for outbound traffic. It must be placed in a public subnet. Private subnet route tables must have a route 0.0.0.0/0 pointing to the NAT Gateway.

questions.question: What is the difference between NAT Gateway and NAT Instance?
questions.answer: NAT Gateway is a fully managed AWS service — highly available, auto-scaling, zero maintenance. NAT Instance is an EC2 you configure yourself to perform NAT — you handle patching, availability, and it is a single point of failure. NAT Gateway is recommended for production. NAT Instance can be cheaper for low-traffic dev/test environments. Security Groups can be attached to NAT Instance but not to NAT Gateway.

questions.question: What is the default Elastic IP limit per region in AWS?
questions.answer: By default, you can have a maximum of 5 Elastic IPs per AWS region per account. You can request a limit increase through AWS Support. This limit exists to conserve the globally limited IPv4 address space, since unattached EIPs waste public IPs.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to troubleshoot a connectivity issue in a private network environment.
questions.answer: (Situation) During a project setup, our application server in a private subnet could not reach the internet to download updates. (Task) I needed to restore outbound internet access while keeping the server unexposed to inbound traffic. (Action) I checked the private subnet's route table and found it only had the local VPC route. I created a NAT Gateway in the public subnet, allocated an Elastic IP for it, and added a route 0.0.0.0/0 → NAT Gateway ID in the private subnet's route table. (Result) The server was able to run package updates within 5 minutes, while remaining inaccessible from the internet.

questions.question: How would you set up secure admin access to 10 private EC2 instances without giving each one a public IP?
questions.answer: (Situation) We had 10 private EC2s with no public IPs that engineers needed to access for debugging. (Task) Enable secure SSH access without exposing any private EC2 to the internet. (Action) I created a single Bastion Host EC2 in the public subnet with an Elastic IP. I configured its Security Group to allow SSH only from our office IP range (/32). Each private EC2's Security Group allowed SSH only from the Bastion's Security Group ID. Engineers SSH into the Bastion, then jump to any private instance. (Result) All 10 instances are accessible securely through one controlled entry point, with all access logged via the Bastion.

questions.question: A customer says they can no longer reach your web server after you restarted it. What happened and how do you fix it permanently?
questions.answer: (Situation) The web server was using a standard public IP. (Task) Diagnose and permanently fix the connectivity issue. (Action) The public IP changed after restart — this is the ephemeral IP behavior. I allocated an Elastic IP, associated it with the EC2 instance, updated the DNS A record to point to the new EIP, and informed the customer to update their firewall rules. (Result) The server now has a fixed IP that will not change on restarts. I also set up a monitoring alert for future restarts.

questions.question: Your company's security policy prohibits opening port 22 from the internet. How do you still allow developers to access private EC2 instances?
questions.answer: (Situation) Security policy banned inbound SSH from internet. Developers still needed shell access to debug issues on private EC2s. (Task) Find a way to provide access without violating policy. (Action) I implemented AWS Systems Manager Session Manager. Verified SSM Agent was installed on all target instances (it is pre-installed on Amazon Linux 2). Created an IAM role with AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore policy and attached it to the instances. Developers now use the AWS Console or CLI to start sessions — no port 22 needed, no public IPs needed. (Result) Full developer access maintained, security policy satisfied, and all sessions are automatically logged to CloudTrail.

questions.question: You launched an EC2 and associated an Elastic IP. You later terminated the instance by accident. What do you do?
questions.answer: (Situation) Instance was accidentally terminated with an Elastic IP associated. (Task) Recover service quickly and preserve the Elastic IP. (Action) Elastic IPs are not deleted when an instance is terminated — they become unassociated and remain in your account. I launched a replacement EC2 instance, then went to Elastic IPs in the console, and associated the same EIP with the new instance. (Result) The Elastic IP is the same, so DNS records and customer firewall rules were unaffected. However, note that EIPs in unattached state incur charges — I moved fast to avoid unexpected billing.

questions.question: How do you decide whether to use Bastion Host or Session Manager for a new project?
questions.answer: (Situation) Designing access strategy for a new multi-tier application. (Task) Choose the access method. (Action) I evaluated both: Bastion Host requires managing an extra EC2, SSH keys, and an open port 22 — it is the traditional approach. Session Manager requires no extra EC2, no open ports, uses IAM for authorization, and provides automatic logging. For new projects in 2024+, Session Manager is the AWS-recommended approach. I use Bastion only when the EC2 doesn't have SSM Agent support or requires RDP with specific configurations. (Result) Chose Session Manager for the project, reducing attack surface and eliminating key management overhead.

questions.question: What happens if you have a NAT Gateway only in one AZ and the EC2 in another AZ needs internet access?
questions.answer: (Situation) Single NAT Gateway in us-east-1a, EC2 in us-east-1b uses it. (Task) Understand the availability risk. (Action) Cross-AZ NAT Gateway usage introduces two risks: a single point of failure (if us-east-1a goes down, us-east-1b loses outbound internet) and additional cross-AZ data transfer charges. Best practice is to deploy one NAT Gateway per AZ and point each AZ's private subnet route table to its local NAT Gateway. (Result) This is a common exam question. The best answer is: one NAT Gateway per AZ for high availability.

questions.question: Your team suggests using NAT Instance to save costs. When is this appropriate?
questions.answer: (Situation) Small team, dev environment, light traffic. (Task) Evaluate NAT Instance vs NAT Gateway. (Action) NAT Instance is appropriate for development/test environments with low traffic (under a few GB/day) where cost is the priority over operational simplicity. It runs on a t2.micro (free tier eligible). However, for production: NAT Gateway is fully managed, auto-scales, highly available within AZ, and requires zero maintenance. I would use NAT Instance only for dev/test, and always document that it needs patching and doesn't auto-scale. (Result) In our dev environment, NAT Instance saved ~$30/month. Production kept NAT Gateway for reliability.

questions.question: A /24 VPC subnet reportedly has only 251 usable IPs. An intern insists it should be 256. How do you explain this?
questions.answer: (Situation) Subnet capacity discussion with a junior engineer. (Task) Explain why 251, not 256. (Action) A /24 CIDR has 256 IP addresses total. AWS reserves 5 per subnet: .0 (network address), .1 (VPC router), .2 (AWS DNS), .3 (reserved for future use), and .255 (broadcast). This leaves 251 usable IPs for EC2 instances and other resources. This is why your professor wrote (251) on the board when discussing a /24 subnet. (Result) The intern understood and I pointed them to the AWS VPC subnet sizing documentation for reference.

questions.question: How would you architect a three-tier application (web, app, database) for security and availability?
questions.answer: (Situation) Three-tier web application design. (Task) Design with proper network security and availability. (Action) Web tier: public subnet, load balancer with public IP (or Elastic IP). EC2 web servers in public subnet. App tier: private subnet, EC2 app servers with only private IPs. Database tier: private subnet, RDS instances with only private IPs. Access: admins use Bastion Host or Session Manager to reach private EC2s. Outbound updates: NAT Gateway in each AZ for app and DB tier. Security Groups: web SG allows 80/443 from internet. App SG allows only from web SG. DB SG allows only from app SG. (Result) Defense-in-depth architecture — even if the web tier is compromised, attackers cannot directly reach app or database tiers.

questions.question: How does NAT Gateway handle state? Why can't the internet initiate connections to instances behind a NAT Gateway?
questions.answer: NAT Gateway is a stateful device — it maintains a connection tracking table that maps outbound connections (private IP + port) to the corresponding EIP + port. When an EC2 in a private subnet initiates an outbound connection, NAT Gateway records this mapping. Return traffic from the internet is matched back to the originating EC2 using this table. Crucially, no entry exists for connections that were never initiated from inside the VPC. So if an external host tries to connect to the NAT Gateway's EIP on an arbitrary port, there is no mapping for it and the connection is dropped. This is why NAT provides both address translation and implicit inbound protection.

questions.question: What are the security group considerations for Bastion Host vs Session Manager?
questions.answer: Bastion Host requires: (1) Bastion SG with inbound SSH (port 22) from trusted IPs only — never 0.0.0.0/0. (2) Private EC2 SG with inbound SSH from Bastion SG ID only. This opens port 22 on the internet-facing Bastion, which is an attack surface. Session Manager requires: no Security Group changes at all — no inbound ports needed. The SSM Agent on the private EC2 makes an outbound HTTPS connection. IAM roles control who can start sessions. This makes Session Manager architecturally more secure — the attack surface is essentially zero for network-level attacks.

questions.question: Explain how Elastic IPs enable blue/green deployments or instant failover in AWS.
questions.answer: In a blue/green or failover scenario, you have two identical environments — one active (blue) and one standby (green). The active server has an Elastic IP. When you need to cut over (deployment or failover), you simply: (1) Disassociate the EIP from the blue instance, (2) Associate it with the green instance. This takes seconds via the AWS API. Because the Elastic IP is the same, all DNS records and customer firewall rules that reference it continue to work immediately — no DNS propagation delay, no customer-side changes. This is especially valuable for compliance-sensitive systems where IPs must be whitelisted.

questions.question: What are the cost implications of having Elastic IPs in a large-scale AWS environment?
questions.answer: At scale, Elastic IPs can generate significant costs if not managed carefully. AWS charges for unattached EIPs (approximately $0.005/hour per IP in most regions). In a large environment with hundreds of EIPs, if any become unattached during scaling events, terminations, or AMI replacements, costs add up quickly. Best practices: (1) Use AWS Config rules to detect unattached EIPs automatically. (2) Set up CloudWatch alarms for EIP count. (3) Prefer AWS-managed solutions (Load Balancers, CloudFront) over individual EC2 EIPs wherever possible. (4) Use Infrastructure as Code (Terraform, CloudFormation) to lifecycle-manage EIPs with their associated instances.

questions.question: How would you design multi-AZ NAT Gateway architecture for a production VPC with three AZs?
questions.answer: For a production VPC with three AZs (e.g., us-east-1a, 1b, 1c), deploy one NAT Gateway per AZ: (1) NAT-GW-1a in the public subnet of AZ-a with EIP-1. (2) NAT-GW-1b in the public subnet of AZ-b with EIP-2. (3) NAT-GW-1c in the public subnet of AZ-c with EIP-3. Each AZ's private subnet route table points 0.0.0.0/0 to its local NAT Gateway. Benefits: (1) If one AZ fails, the other AZs are unaffected. (2) No cross-AZ data transfer charges. (3) Better performance — traffic stays within the AZ. Trade-off: Three times the NAT Gateway cost. For cost-sensitive environments, use a single NAT Gateway with awareness of the single-AZ availability risk.
